subject: mathematics
question_text: Find the angles made by the straight line passing through the points (1, −3, 2) and (3, −5, 1) with the coordinate axes.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.64, chapter 6 ADDITION OF VECTORS, Short Answer question 6(iii). Only the question was taken — the solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work, see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The direction vector is AB = 2i − 2j − k with |AB| = 3, so the direction cosines are 2/3, −2/3, −1/3 and the angles are Cos⁻¹(2/3), Cos⁻¹(−2/3), Cos⁻¹(−1/3). Checked a second way with the identity l² + m² + n² = (4 + 4 + 1)/9 = 1. A line has two opposite directions, so BA gives the three supplementary angles; the card states that rather than leaving it unsaid, because a student whose answer reads Cos⁻¹(−2/3), Cos⁻¹(2/3), Cos⁻¹(1/3) has not made an error. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 split rewards the four separate acts: the direction vector, its magnitude, the direction cosines, and the angles written as inverse cosines. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern; Addition of Vectors has no Section C slot on the paper, so the unit is SAQ and VSAQ only. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the angles a line makes with the axes — say what you build from the two points and what you do with it.

steps.label: Find the direction vector
steps.margin_note: First mark. The line is fixed by its direction, and the direction of a line through two points is the vector joining them. Subtract coordinate by coordinate.
steps.memory_tip: The direction of a line through two points is the second point minus the first, coordinate by coordinate.
lines: AB is a direction vector of the line.

recall.must_convey: That AB = OB − OA = 2i − 2j − k is taken as the direction vector of the line.
accept: the direction vector is B minus A which is two i minus two j minus k
subtract the position vectors of the two points
AB is OB minus OA and that gives the direction of the line
AB ante OB minus OA, two i minus two j minus k vasthundi
take the vector joining the two given points
heard_as: two i minus two j minus k

steps.why: Angles with the axes depend only on which way the line points, not on where it sits. Any vector along the line carries that information, and the join of the two given points is the easiest one to build.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the wrong way round, which reverses all three signs.
A sign slip on the y term, where the coordinate is already negative.

steps.label: Find its magnitude
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Square each component with its sign, add, take the square root. The 9 here is exact, so the direction cosines come out as neat thirds.
steps.memory_tip: Square each component with its sign, add, then take the square root. Here it is an exact 3.

accept: the magnitude is the square root of four plus four plus one which is three
root nine is three
take the modulus of the direction vector
magnitude root nine ante three
square the components add them and take the root

steps.why: Direction cosines are the components of a vector of length 1, so the length of the direction vector is what every component must be divided by.
common_mistakes: Writing (−2)² as −4 by squaring only the 2.
Adding the components instead of their squares.

steps.label: Write the direction cosines
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Divide each component by the magnitude. Keep the minus signs — they are what say the line points backwards along the y and z axes.
steps.memory_tip: Divide every component by the length. Keep the minus signs, and check l² + m² + n² = 1.
lines: The direction cosines are the components
of the unit vector along AB:

recall.must_convey: That dividing each component by 3 gives the direction cosines l = 2/3, m = −2/3, n = −1/3, and that their squares add to 1.
accept: divide each component by three to get two thirds minus two thirds and minus one third
the direction cosines are the components of the unit vector
the squares of the three direction cosines add up to one
prathi component ni three tho divide cheste direction cosines vasthai
keep the minus signs on the second and third ones

steps.why: A unit vector's components are the cosines of the angles it makes with the axes, because each component is the projection of a length of 1 onto that axis. The identity l² + m² + n² = 1 is a free check on the arithmetic.
common_mistakes: Dropping the minus signs and reporting all three cosines as positive.

steps.label: State the three angles
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Turn each cosine into an angle and say which axis each one belongs to. A negative cosine gives an obtuse angle, which is correct, not an error to be tidied away.
steps.memory_tip: One angle per axis, in the order x, y, z. A negative cosine simply means an obtuse angle.
lines: Let α, β, γ be the angles the line makes
with the x, y and z axes. Then
cos α = 2/3,  cos β = −2/3,  cos γ = −1/3
Taking BA instead reverses all three signs

recall.must_convey: That the angles with the x, y and z axes are Cos⁻¹(2/3), Cos⁻¹(−2/3) and Cos⁻¹(−1/3).
accept: the angles are cos inverse two thirds cos inverse minus two thirds and cos inverse minus one third
each direction cosine becomes an angle by taking the inverse cosine
the angle with the y axis is obtuse because its cosine is negative
cos inverse teeskunte angles vasthai, x y z axes tho
the opposite direction gives the supplementary angles

steps.why: The question asked for angles, not cosines, so the inverse cosine is the last required step. A line has two opposite directions, so the second set of answers is equally correct and worth naming.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as the direction cosines and never writing the angles.
Making all three angles acute by dropping the minus signs.
Pairing the angles with the wrong axes.
